column4: This is the section's explicit Qur'anic meeting: setting the face to dīn, God-given fiṭra, unaltered khalq, and الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ bind formed nature to upright religion.
أَقِيمُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ and مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ join upright orientation and sincere obedience with “as He began you, you return,” making creation, religion, and return one movement.
The best dīn is embodied by one who submits his face to God, does good, and follows Abraham as a ḥanīf; this enacts the section's link between upright religion and righteous conduct.
Abraham directs his face as a ḥanīf to the One who فَطَرَ the heavens and earth, directly joining primordial making, orientation, and monotheistic religion.
The command أَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ حَنِيفًا is a close parallel to the section's central command and makes uprightness an active religious stance.
The commanded declaration دِينًا قِيَمًا مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ حَنِيفًا is the section's cited formulation of upright religion.
Worship with sincere dīn, prayer, and almsgiving are gathered under دِينُ الْقَيِّمَةِ, so upright religion becomes a pattern of acts.
أَقِمْ وَجْهَكَ لِلدِّينِ الْقَيِّمِ repeats the face-and-upright-dīn scene and adds the deadline of the unavoidable Day.
Exclusive worship under God's judgment is identified as الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ, defining upright religion as obedience rather than an abstract label.
The ordained measure of sacred months and the command not to wrong oneself are called الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ, giving upright religion a just ordering of conduct and time.
أَقِيمُوا الدِّينَ وَلَا تَتَفَرَّقُوا فِيهِ turns the q-w-m family into a command to uphold one religion without division.
فَاسْتَقِمْ كَمَا أُمِرْتَ makes prophetic uprightness obedience to command and couples it with belief in revelation and equitable judgment.
خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّاكَ فَعَدَلَكَ is the closest creation scene: God creates, proportionally forms, and balances the human before the passage names denial of dīn.
كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِالدِّينِ completes 82:7-8's formed-human scene with the same denial of dīn that closes this section.
فَاسْتَقِيمُوا إِلَيْهِ commands a straight course toward the one God, closely realizing the section's definition of human istiqāma as adhering to the upright way.
Belief and righteous deeds receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, the exact reward formula of 95:6 within a passage that has just commanded istiqāma.
أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ exactly repeats the unending-reward phrase and directly precedes the Qur'an's description of the Prophet's khuluq.
خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ uses the source section's khalq-family sense “inborn character”; beside 68:3 it joins character to the same unending reward as 95:6.
The full exception “those who believe and do righteous deeds” and أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ exactly reproduce 95:6 after a scene of denial.
اللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ ... وَمِنْكُمْ مَنْ يُرَدُّ إِلَى أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ directly joins human creation, divine returning, and the lowest stage of age.
وَمَنْ نُعَمِّرْهُ نُنَكِّسْهُ فِي الْخَلْقِ states the physical reversal of created form that the section's return to the lowest can carry.
God creates from weakness, gives strength, then after strength appoints weakness and grey age; the rise and reversal spell out the human arc compressed in 95:4-5.
The staged making from dust, drop, clot, and womb ends with some being returned to the feeblest age, a detailed creation-and-decline counterpart to 95:4-5.
Hypocrites occupy الدَّرْكِ الْأَسْفَلِ, a moral and eschatological realization of “lowest,” whose exception is supplied in the next ayah.
The exception to the lowest depth is repentance, إصلاح, holding fast to God, and making dīn sincere; they are placed with believers who receive reward, closely matching 95:5-6.
The ayah explicitly joins attempts to يَرُدُّوكُمْ عَنْ دِينِكُمْ with whoever يَرْتَدِدْ ... عَنْ دِينِهِ, the section's cited religious sense of the r-d-d family.
لَوْ يَرُدُّونَكُمْ مِنْ بَعْدِ إِيمَانِكُمْ كُفَّارًا supplies the section's exact return-after-faith relation and makes the reversal an intended pressure from others.
يَرُدُّوكُمْ بَعْدَ إِيمَانِكُمْ كَافِرِينَ places r-d-d, “after,” faith, and unbelief in one warning, as the prose explicitly observes.
مَنْ يَرْتَدَّ مِنْكُمْ عَنْ دِينِهِ names apostasy directly, then promises that God will bring a faithful people in the apostates' place.
Those who ارْتَدُّوا عَلَى أَدْبَارِهِمْ after guidance became clear embody a backward movement away from an already disclosed straight course.
أَنْقَلَبْتُمْ عَلَى أَعْقَابِكُمْ and “whoever turns back on his heels” stage religious regression as bodily reversal while affirming that it cannot harm God.
The Book is قَيِّمًا so that it warns and gives believers who do righteous deeds news of a good reward, joining upright guidance and the 95:6 response.
Revelation and the balance are sent لِيَقُومَ النَّاسُ بِالْقِسْطِ: religion makes people stand in justice, almost a Qur'anic enactment of the source dictionary's qiwām and upright conduct.
God is قَائِمًا بِالْقِسْطِ, maintaining justice, and the next ayah names Islam as the dīn before Him; q-w-m and justice meet exactly as in the source definition.
الدِّينَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ الْإِسْلَامُ identifies religion with submission immediately after God is described as standing in justice.
كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ بِالْقِسْطِ commands believers to stand persistently for justice even against self and kin, carrying uprightness into moral action.
كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ لِلَّهِ ... بِالْقِسْطِ makes standing for God and just witness the conduct nearest to taqwā.
Measured spending between extravagance and stinginess is قَوَامًا, directly exemplifying the source dictionary's qawām as just balance.
أُمَّةٌ قَائِمَةٌ describes an upright community whose night recitation and prostration make q-w-m a settled religious disposition.
The upright community believes, commands right, forbids wrong, and hastens in good deeds; this ayah supplies the conduct by which 3:113's standing is known.
Those who hold fast to the Book and أَقَامُوا الصَّلَاةَ are called مُصْلِحِينَ, and God does not waste their reward; adherence, q-w-m, reform, and recompense meet here.
قَوَّامُونَ uses q-w-m for sustained care and responsibility within a household, directly illustrating the source dictionary's “one who manages and sets a people right.”
Wealth is something God made قِيَامًا for people, a concrete Qur'anic instance of the source sense “that by which something stands.”
The Kaaba is made قِيَامًا لِلنَّاسِ, extending q-w-m from bodily uprightness to an institution that sustains communal life.
Submitting one's face to God while doing good yields secure reward; inward surrender, outward ṣalāḥ, orientation, and recompense align in one sentence.
One who يُسْلِمْ وَجْهَهُ إِلَى اللَّهِ while doing good has grasped the firmest handle, picturing upright religion as submission and stable support.
Once right guidance is distinct from error, belief in God is grasping الْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَى; the unbreakable support makes the section's “religion by which one stands” visible.
هَذَا صِرَاطِي مُسْتَقِيمًا فَاتَّبِعُوهُ explicitly turns the upright method into a path one must follow and contrasts it with diverging ways.
God makes believers firm with الْقَوْلِ الثَّابِتِ and leads wrongdoers astray, specifying divine agency in steadfastness and moral displacement.
Faith is denied until people accept the Prophet's judgment, feel no inner resistance, and submit fully; this closely explicates īmān as the soul's assent and surrender to truth.
The distinction between merely saying “we believe” and faith entering the hearts sharpens the section's definition of īmān as inward assent, while obedience is named as its operative test.
The creation of jinn and humans is given the purpose of worship, directly placing created being on the line of religious obedience.
The command to worship “your Lord who created you” makes human creation itself the ground for obedience and taqwā.
“Our Lord is He who gave each thing its created form, then guided it” states the section's core movement from fitted creation to direction.
مِنْ نُطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ joins creation and measured fitting in the human body.
ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ follows measured creation with an eased way, making bodily formation and directed course consecutive.
الَّذِي خَلَقَ فَسَوَّى presents creation as proportioning and fitting, a close parallel to “the best taqwīm.”
وَالَّذِي قَدَّرَ فَهَدَى continues fitted creation with measure and guidance, the same creation-to-direction relation developed in the prose.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it makes moral life rest upon a divinely fitted human self.
The fitted soul is inspired with both its corruption and its taqwā, locating the moral fork inside the creation scene of 91:7.
Success belongs to one who purifies that divinely formed soul, showing created capacity carried into upright action.
Failure belongs to one who buries or corrupts that soul, the specific reversal of preserving its given moral direction.
God creates the human from a mixed drop as a test and equips him with hearing and sight, joining formation and moral purpose.
After created equipment, God guides the way and the human becomes grateful or ungrateful; this states the movement from fit creation to chosen stance.
إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ خُلِقَ هَلُوعًا names an anxious created disposition, directly activating the prose's khalq/khuluq relation between constitution and character.
Distress makes that created anxious person panic, specifying how the disposition of 70:19 appears in conduct.
Good fortune makes that person withholding, completing the behavioral portrait before the exception for worshippers.
إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ interrupts the general human disposition with a religious exception, structurally paralleling 95:6's exception for believers who act rightly.
The universal statement that the human is in loss provides a moral descent corresponding to the return to the lowest.
The exception for those who believe, do righteous deeds, and sustain truth and patience closely parallels the rescuing exception of 95:6.
أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ بِالدِّينِ turns denial of dīn into a question whose answer is displayed in habitual conduct.
Repelling the orphan is the first concrete act by which 107:1's denial of dīn is recognized, supporting the section's link between religion and character.
Failure to urge feeding the poor gives denial of dīn a second social and habitual expression.
The warning to worshippers begins a boundary between the outward religious act and the upright disposition the act should embody.
Heedlessness toward prayer shows a religious practice severed from settled obedience.
Showing off makes the religious act serve social display rather than sincere dīn.
Withholding even small aid completes the surah's demonstration that denial of dīn is disclosed by corrupted conduct.
أَحْسَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ says God made everything He created good and immediately begins the creation of the human, closely echoing best-created form.
وَصَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ explicitly says God formed humans and made their forms good, then calls them to the Lord of the worlds.
خَلَقَ ... وَصَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ joins creation in truth, beautiful human form, and final destination.
The creation of death and life is for testing أَيُّكُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا, placing “best” created order in direct relation to the quality of deeds.
The human created from a drop becomes a manifest opponent, a sharp creation-to-denial reversal resembling the section's movement from formation to denying dīn.
The opponent forgets his own creation while challenging resurrection, specifying the failure of inference that the section's rhetorical question exposes.
The answer appeals to the One who created the first time, making original creation the proof of return and judgment.
“Did you think We created you aimlessly and that you would not be returned?” directly makes created purpose entail return and accountability.
God created heavens and earth in truth so that every soul may be repaid for what it earned; creation, just measure, and judgment form one claim.
The question whether the human expects to be left purposeless opens a creation argument for accountability.
The human's origin as an emitted drop supplies the first stage of that accountability argument.
ثُمَّ كَانَ عَلَقَةً فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّى makes creation and proportioning the decisive middle of the argument.
Making the human pair male and female displays the completed created order under discussion.
The closing question infers God's power to revive the dead from the fitted creation just recounted, paralleling the move from creation to dīn as judgment.
اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ makes the Creator the ground of the first command addressed to the Prophet.
خَلَقَ الْإِنْسَانَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ identifies the human creation at the start of a passage that soon exposes human transgression.
كَلَّا إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَيَطْغَى turns from created-and-taught humanity to its moral descent, a close structural reversal of fitted creation.
The human transgresses because he sees himself self-sufficient, naming the disposition behind the fall.
إِنَّ إِلَى رَبِّكَ الرُّجْعَى answers self-sufficiency with inevitable return, restoring the Creator's authority over human direction.
Seeking a dīn other than God's is confronted with the willing or unwilling submission of everything in heavens and earth and its return to Him; created order and religion coincide.
A dīn other than islām is rejected, and its seeker loses in the Hereafter, setting a firm boundary around religion as submission.
Turning away from Abraham's milla is called self-stultification, while his election and righteousness state the fit between sound self and upright religion.
Abraham answers the command “submit” with submission to the Lord of the worlds, enacting dīn as obedience.
Abraham and Jacob charge their children to remain in the chosen dīn until death as submitters, making steadfastness a transmitted way of life.
Striving, the religion without constriction, Abraham's milla, being named Muslims, prayer, charity, and holding fast to God make dīn a sustaining whole.
True believers answer God's judgment with “we hear and obey,” a direct behavioral expression of faith as assent and dīn as obedience.
خُلُقُ الْأَوَّلِينَ denotes the habitual way of former peoples, a Qur'anic use of the khalq family in precisely the character/custom field developed in the prose.
“Each acts according to his شَاكِلَتِهِ” states nonlexically that settled formation or disposition takes visible form in action.
When told not to spread corruption, the offenders claim إِنَّمَا نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ, posing the exact ṣalāḥ/fasād opposition as a dispute about conduct.
God identifies those professed reformers as the actual corrupters, supplying the judgment missing from their self-description.
In conduct toward orphans, إِصْلَاحٌ is better and God knows الْمُفْسِدَ مِنَ الْمُصْلِحِ, directly defining the action-level opposition named by the source.
The powerful offenders يُفْسِدُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا يُصْلِحُونَ, an exact Qur'anic pairing of corruption with failure to act rightly.
Doing good as God has done good is opposed to seeking corruption on earth, locating ṣalāḥ's contrary in chosen action.
Corruption appears through what people's hands have earned so that they taste consequences and perhaps return; conduct deforms order and is meant to prompt reversal.
The command not to corrupt the earth بَعْدَ إِصْلَاحِهَا makes fasād a reversal after established ṣalāḥ, closely matching the section's concern with falling away after right formation.
After disbelief following faith, repentance and أَصْلَحُوا reopen mercy, showing that religious reversal can itself be answered by moral repair.
Forgiveness is promised to one who repents, believes, acts rightly, and then remains guided, gathering the section's inward assent, صالح action, and continued direction.
Satan's command that people فَلَيُغَيِّرُنَّ خَلْقَ اللَّهِ directly opposes 30:30's “no alteration in God's creation,” the section's key boundary between given fiṭra and its attempted distortion.
When the people deviate, God causes their hearts to deviate; this reverses istiqāma and highlights the divine agency also present in “We returned him.”
The Book has no عِوَجًا, and 18:2 calls it قَيِّمًا; crookedness and uprightness form an explicit boundary in revealed guidance.
خُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ ضَعِيفًا qualifies “best taqwīm”: good fitted creation does not erase the human constitution's weakness.
خُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ مِنْ عَجَلٍ gives haste as a created human tendency, a specific boundary on reading best formation as perfected conduct.
لَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الْإِنْسَانَ فِي كَبَدٍ places human creation in toil, a bodily-life boundary to the claim of best taqwīm.
The human is created from a drop and then becomes a manifest disputant; the moral posture sharply reverses the humility implied by his origin.
People make dīn sincere to God in danger and then transgress after rescue, showing a temporary religious state rather than the stable disposition the section calls upright.
Shipwreck fear produces sincere dīn, but deliverance produces renewed association; the scene dramatizes failure to remain on the confessed direction.
Calling God with sincere dīn in enveloping waves is followed by divided responses on land, with only some remaining measured and steadfast.
Pharaoh fears Moses will change “your dīn” or cause corruption, exposing dīn as an established public order while inverting who actually embodies fasād.
Turning away is pictured as spreading corruption and severing kinship, making religious retreat visible in anti-ṣalāḥ acts.
لَا تَرْتَدُّوا عَلَى أَدْبَارِكُمْ uses the r-d-d family for literal retreat from a commanded advance, the bodily image underlying apostasy's backward turn.
The source dictionary cites al-khalāq as “religion,” whereas مَا لَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ مِنْ خَلَاقٍ here means no allotted share in the Hereafter; the same form marks a necessary semantic boundary.
مَا لَهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ مِنْ خَلَاقٍ again uses khalāq for an afterlife share, distinct from the source's cited dictionary sense “religion.”
لَا خَلَاقَ لَهُمْ فِي الْآخِرَةِ uses khalāq as allotted portion, a specific Qur'anic counter-sense to the lexical value “religion” named in the section.

خَلَاق names the worldly share enjoyed by earlier peoples and their imitators; its “portion” sense differs from the source gloss “religion,” while imitation makes an inherited way of life part of the warning.
The question “what deceived you concerning your generous Lord?” opens the creation-to-denial sequence and parallels the section's challenge “what then makes you deny?”
God composes the human in whatever form He wills, completing 82:7's shaping before 82:9's accusation of denying dīn.
Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are declared wholly for God immediately after the announcement of the upright dīn, expanding religion into an entire lived state.
The rejection of partners and command to be first among those who submit completes the stance introduced by dīnan qiyaman in 6:161.
Turning penitently to God, taqwā, prayer, and refusal of shirk specify the conduct of the fiṭra and upright dīn named in 30:30.
After the command to set the face to upright religion, disbelief is charged to the disbeliever while righteous action is something people prepare for themselves.
God's rewarding of believers who do righteous deeds completes the consequence of standing toward the upright religion in 30:43.
Withholding alms and denying the Hereafter supply the contrary conduct between the command to be straight in 41:6 and the unending reward in 41:8.
مَاكِثِينَ فِيهِ أَبَدًا makes the good reward announced with the upright Book in 18:2 explicitly enduring, paralleling ghayr mamnūn.
God raises the heaven and sets the balance, presenting upright created order as measured equilibrium.
The prohibition against transgressing the balance turns cosmic measure into a boundary for human behavior.
أَقِيمُوا الْوَزْنَ بِالْقِسْطِ commands people to establish weight justly, joining q-w-m, measure, and justice in action.
الْقَيُّومُ names God as the self-subsisting sustainer, the ultimate q-w-m sense behind the section's idea of that by which created life and truth stand.
Heaven and earth تَقُومَانِ بِأَمْرِهِ, showing the created cosmos held standing by divine command before humans are called forth.
God is قَائِمٌ عَلَى كُلِّ نَفْسٍ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ, combining q-w-m oversight with each person's deeds and thus approaching the source's governor sense.
Remaining straight عَلَى الطَّرِيقَةِ is answered with abundant provision, a direct instance of istiqāma as staying on the established way.
فَاسْتَقِمْ كَمَا أُمِرْتَ commands the Prophet and repentant companions to remain upright and not transgress.
Those who say “our Lord is God” and then اسْتَقَامُوا embody settled confession carried into continued uprightness.
The same confession followed by اسْتَقَامُوا brings freedom from fear and grief, emphasizing permanence in the religious course.
Moses and Aaron are told فَاسْتَقِيمَا and not to follow the way of the ignorant, making steadfastness obedience after answered prayer.
فَمَا اسْتَقَامُوا لَكُمْ فَاسْتَقِيمُوا لَهُمْ applies istiqāma to faithful treaty conduct, a concrete social use of upright human behavior.
Holding fast to revelation is warranted because the addressee is عَلَى صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ, linking adherence to the upright path.
Holding fast to God leads to صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ, expressing the support-and-straight-way relation without the source's exact vocabulary of religion.
Belief and holding fast to God lead into a straight path, joining inward faith, stable support, and direction.
The answer to sectarian religious claims is Abraham's milla as a ḥanīf, a direct companion to 6:161's upright religion.
The command to follow Abraham's ḥanīf milla gives concrete content to the upright religion named in 6:161.
Revelation commands the Prophet to follow Abraham's milla as a ḥanīf, repeating the prophetic stance behind the section's qiyam dīn.
The intervening profession believes in the revelations to Abraham and the prophets without division, specifying the submission whose exclusive validity 3:85 states.
Worshipping God مُخْلِصًا لَهُ الدِّينَ defines dīn as sincere obedience in a direct command.
The Prophet is commanded to worship God while making dīn sincere, reinforcing religion as an enacted submission.
Everything in heavens and earth belongs to God and وَلَهُ الدِّينُ وَاصِبًا describes enduring obedience, bringing dīn close to a permanent state.
دِينِ الْمَلِكِ means the king's governing law or order, a Qur'anic instance of dīn as an established way of affairs rather than creed alone.
The question asks how God would guide people who disbelieved after their faith despite bearing witness and receiving clear proofs, specifying the “after belief” regression.
Disbelief after faith is distinguished from coerced speech with a heart secure in faith, sharpening the section's inward definition of īmān and the boundary of apostasy.
The human's creation through successive stages to maturity and old age expands the bodily arc between formation and decline.
The embryo is successively formed and then produced as another creation, ending with praise of the best of creators; it concretizes excellent human formation.
Death follows the detailed formation of 23:12-14, marking the created body's downward boundary.
Resurrection after death completes the formation-to-return sequence and brings the human before judgment.
The children of Adam are honored, carried, provided for, and favored over much creation, a status parallel to best human taqwīm.
The gift of two eyes begins a bodily-endowment argument that turns immediately toward moral direction.
A tongue and two lips continue the inventory of fitted human capacities.
Guidance to the two heights or paths converts created faculties into moral alternatives.
The human nevertheless does not cross the steep path, showing failure to use the given formation in its right direction.
The steep path culminates in being among believers who counsel patience and mercy, supplying the faith-and-conduct side of the scene.
After God fashions the human and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, “little are you grateful” makes moral response the test of fitted form.
Humans leave the womb knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts so that they may be grateful, linking created equipment to a religious response.
God produces humans and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, yet they give little thanks; fitted faculties and failed disposition stand together.
God's “coloring” is claimed as unsurpassed while the speakers declare worship, a nonlexical image of divinely given formation expressed as religion.
The speaker asks why he should not worship the One who فَطَرَنِي and to whom all return, making origination the reason for dīn.
Abraham rejects inherited objects of worship except الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي, trusting that his Maker will guide him; formation and direction meet in a polemic against custom.
Whoever acts rightly while believing receives a good life and reward by the best of their deeds, extending the section's faith-and-ṣalāḥ consequence.
Male or female believers who act rightly enter the Garden and receive provision without reckoning, a close reward parallel to 95:6.
God does not destroy communities unjustly while their people are مُصْلِحُونَ, showing reform as conduct that keeps collective life standing.
The Qur'an guides to الَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ and gives believers who do righteous deeds news of great reward, directly joining the q-w-m superlative, guidance, faith, action, and recompense.
إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّى announces divergent human courses, opening a compact scene of opposed dispositions and divinely eased destinations.
Giving and guarding oneself supply the first acts of the upright course in 92:4-7.
Affirming “the best” adds inward assent to that course, closely pairing conviction with conduct.
God's “We shall ease him toward ease” makes divine direction answer the person's faith-shaped conduct.
Stinginess and imagined self-sufficiency begin the contrary disposition, reversing giving and taqwā.
Denying “the best” supplies the unbelieving counterpart to 92:6's assent.
God's “We shall ease him toward hardship” is a striking parallel to divine return toward the lowest after the human chooses denial.
The test distinguishes one who follows the Messenger from one who يَنْقَلِبُ عَلَى عَقِبَيْهِ, staging religious reversal as turning back on the heels.
Obeying the disbelievers would يَرُدُّوكُمْ عَلَى أَعْقَابِكُمْ and turn believers into losers, directly combining external reversal, backward motion, and religious loss.
Disbelieving after faith and then increasing in disbelief is a repeated formulation of the section's regression “after belief,” with repentance no longer credited as sincere.
Darkened faces are asked, “Did you disbelieve after your faith?”, giving the after-faith reversal its judgment-day manifestation.
The declaration “you disbelieved after your faith” is another exact religious reversal, here exposed after mockery rather than external coercion.
The ayah says the offenders disbelieved after their islām, another direct formulation of leaving a previously assumed religious state.
One who worships God “on an edge” turns his face back when tested and loses both worlds, the opposite of setting the face firmly to upright religion.
Guardians placed over people follow the accusation of denying dīn and begin the passage's account of how conduct is preserved for judgment.
The guardians are noble recording scribes, making deeds rather than profession alone the evidence relevant to dīn.
The recorders know what people do, completing the bridge from formed creation and denial to accountable action.
The righteous are in bliss, giving ṣalāḥ its judgment-side outcome after 82:9's denial of dīn.
The wicked are in the Blaze, the contrary outcome paired with 82:13's righteous.
The question “what will make you know what the Day of dīn is?” fixes judgment or recompense as the immediate contextual sense of dīn in 82:9, a vital boundary beside the section's religion reading.
Repeating the question intensifies the identification of dīn with the coming Day rather than merely a present communal religion.
On that Day no soul controls anything for another and command belongs to God, supplying the content of dīn as final judgment.
الَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ repeats denial of dīn explicitly as denial of Judgment Day.
Only every transgressing sinner denies that Day, tying denial to a settled moral condition.
Calling recited signs “legends of the ancients” gives the denier's stance and speech concrete form.
What people repeatedly earned has rusted over their hearts, a vivid account of actions becoming an inward disposition.
The condemned say they were not among those who prayed, beginning a conduct-based explanation that culminates in denial of the Day of dīn.
They did not feed the poor, pairing failed worship with failed social action as in the behavioral exposure of dīn-denial.
They joined vain or wrongful discourse with those who indulged in it, showing a habitual social course.
“We used to deny the Day of dīn” names the belief that corresponds to the preceding corrupt practices.
Their pattern continued until certainty came, emphasizing persistence in the denying disposition rather than a momentary lapse.
Creating the human from an extract of clay supplies the first material stage of the excellent formation completed in 23:14.
Placement as a drop in a secure resting place supplies the next stage and the protected setting of human formation.
When mercy is removed, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful, beginning a portrait of unstable disposition under changing conditions.
After hardship is replaced by favor, the same human becomes exultant and boastful, showing his state pulled about by circumstance.
The exception is those who remain patient and do righteous deeds, for whom are forgiveness and great reward; this closely parallels 95:6's exception and reward.
The worshippers excepted from anxious human disposition are constant in prayer, making steadiness itself the distinguishing religious habit.
Those formed by the intervening faithful practices are honored in gardens, supplying the endpoint opposite anxious and withholding conduct.
Success belongs to the one who purifies himself, a direct moral response to the created-and-guided human scene earlier in the surah.
Remembering the Lord's name and praying turns purification into concrete religious conduct.
Preferring the nearer life is the contrary orientation, explaining how a guided creature chooses the lower horizon.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, setting enduring recompense against the preference in 87:16 and illuminating “unending reward.”
The criminal who comes to his Lord has Hell, where he neither dies nor lives, an extreme low destination for a corrupted course.
The one who comes as a believer having done righteous deeds receives the highest degrees, a direct high/low reversal built from the same faith-and-action pair as 95:6.
Everlasting gardens complete the believer's high reward and clarify the enduring side of that contrast.
A person given God's signs slips out of them and follows Satan, a precise scene of abandoning an already granted direction.
God could have raised him by the signs, but he clings to earth and follows desire; height and self-chosen lowness sharply illuminate the return toward the lowest.
Those who believe, act righteously, and affirm the revealed truth have their evils removed and their state أَصْلَحَ بَالَهُمْ; God actively rectifies the believing people.
Holding together to God's rope and refusing division makes religion a sustaining bond by which a people stands, complementing “establish the dīn and do not divide.”
God's repelling of some people by others prevents monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques from being demolished, showing divine support keeping worship standing in the world.
Those established in the land establish prayer, give alms, command right, and forbid wrong, showing q-w-m authority used to rectify communal conduct.
Supporting God's cause brings divine support and firm feet, a concrete image of religion as that by which believers remain standing.
Full measure and weight with justice, just speech, and covenant-keeping immediately precede the command to follow God's straight path, embodying upright religion as equitable acts.
Full measure and weighing with الْقِسْطَاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ make straightness a standard of practical justice.
Full measure and weight and the ban on corruption after the earth's reform join just ordering with the exact ṣalāḥ/fasād reversal.
Just measure and weight are commanded together with a ban on depriving people and spreading corruption, making qawām-like justice the opposite of fasād.
Giving full measure and refusing to cause loss opens a three-ayah picture of upright commercial conduct.
Weighing with the straight balance explicitly joins istiqāma and justice.
Not diminishing people's goods and not roaming as corrupters supplies the fasād boundary of the preceding straight measure.
The Qur'an is Arabic غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ, “without crookedness,” a direct negative boundary around the upright revealed way.
A powerless dependent is contrasted with one who commands justice and stands on a straight path, linking ability to set affairs right, equity, and upright direction.

People “fabricate falsehood” and worship powerless idols, whereas provision, worship, gratitude, and return belong to God; the khalq root's fabrication sense is set against divine origination and true dīn.
God says He created and shaped humanity before commanding the angels to prostrate to Adam, adding bestowed dignity to the formed-human scene.
God's fashioning of the human and breathing into him precede the angels' prostration, a specific image of completed form and honor.
“Stand before God devoutly obedient” makes bodily standing a direct enactment of dīn as obedience.
One who is devout through the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for mercy, embodies a settled religious state in literal posture.
“The pure dīn belongs to God” distinguishes sincere obedience from the patronage offered to intermediaries.
The Prophet is told to worship God while making his dīn sincere, repeating religion as a personally enacted submission.
Calling upon God with dīn made sincere, even against unbelievers' dislike, presents obedience as an undivided stance.
The living God alone is invoked with sincere dīn, grounding enduring obedience in the One who does not die.
“To you your dīn and to me mine” marks a firm boundary between established religious ways after repeated refusal to exchange worship.
Joseph addresses the Creator of heavens and earth as his protector and asks to die in submission and join the righteous, joining origination, dīn, ṣalāḥ, and life's end.
The magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh over clear proofs and الَّذِي فَطَرَنَا, making loyalty to the One who formed them govern their religious choice.
The messengers appeal to God as Originator of heavens and earth who calls people for forgiveness, connecting creation with the summons to repent.
The people are told to fear the One who created them and former generations, grounding taqwā in created dependence.
Ṣāliḥ commands worship of the God who produced people from the earth and settled them in it, then calls for forgiveness and repentance; origin and religious return meet.
“He created you in stages” states ordered human formation in compact form.
God causing humans to grow from the earth like a growth gives organic form to created constitution.
God then returns people to the earth and brings them forth again, completing formation with divinely governed return.
Traveling the earth to see how creation began is made evidence that God will produce the later creation, linking origin to accountability.
God's lack of weariness in the first creation exposes human doubt about a new creation, another creation-to-return argument.
Repenting after wrongdoing and doing iṣlāḥ makes moral repair the answer to a fallen course.
Whoever does evil in ignorance and afterward repents and reforms receives mercy, pairing “after” with recovery through iṣlāḥ.
Wrongdoing in ignorance followed by repentance and reform is again answered with forgiveness, a repeated route back from corrupted action.
True believers are those whose faith is not followed by doubt and whose striving proves it, sharpening faith as settled assent expressed in acts.
A believing man or woman has no contrary choice once God and His Messenger decide; disobedience is manifest straying, so faith is defined through submission.
Righteousness is unfolded as belief, giving, prayer, alms, covenant-keeping, and patience, showing how inward faith becomes a stable pattern of صالح conduct.
Whomever God guides has the breast opened to islām, while misguidance makes it constricted, locating religious direction in the inward human state under divine agency.
A breast opened to islām and light from God is contrasted with hardened hearts, another precise link between dīn and settled inner disposition.
The revelation is a reminder, so whoever wills may take a way to the Lord; this continues the created-and-guided human scene of 76:2-3.
Human willing is placed within God's will, clarifying the divine agency behind taking or leaving the directed way.
Breaking God's covenant after binding it, severing commanded bonds, and spreading corruption show a sustained religious order deliberately undone in action.
